title: Starting work
tomorrow: pray at set times or anytime? which does the Church pick?

segments.voice: Yesterday, on the way: a crowd that stopped for one man by the road. The line was a daily pilgrimage.

Trays to wipe, boxes to fold, a mop leaning on the wall. Nobody posts their first hour of work. But Paul wrote a line that says even that hour can be holy, and the odd thing is where he put it. In the Douay-Rheims: "whether you eat or drink, or whatsoever else you do, do all to the glory of God." The glory of God. And he starts with lunch.
screen: `TRAYS, BOXES, A MOP.` → `DO ALL TO THE GLORY OF GOD.` → `HE STARTS WITH LUNCH.`

segments.voice: So why open with eating and drinking? Read the chapter around it and the answer is almost funny. Paul is answering a practical question from the church in Corinth: is it all right to eat meat that came from a pagan temple, say at a friend's dinner? He works through it case by case. Then he pulls the lens all the way back: whether you eat or drink, or whatsoever else you do. The plainest thing on the list is the one he names first. If a meal can be offered, so can anything. He says it again to the Colossians: "All whatsoever you do in word or in work, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ." In word or in work. The monks took that literally. The Rule of Saint Benedict calls idleness the enemy of the soul and sets hours for work and hours for holy reading inside the same day, one after the other. So offered work isn't a different job. It's the same tray, the same inbox, with one thing added at the start: whom it's for. And the start is the easy place to add it, before the rest of the day crowds in. One to tell a friend: Paul's great line about the glory of God comes out of an argument about what to eat at dinner.
screen: `WHY START WITH EATING?` · `A QUESTION ABOUT TEMPLE MEAT.` · `IN WORD OR IN WORK.` · `SAME TASK, ONE THING ADDED.` · then, large: `OFFERED WORK.`

segments.voice: Name the very first task waiting for you tomorrow, the plainest one. Rest your hands on your knees, palms up, as if you were holding it. Offer it there, with Paul's words, do all to the glory of God, or with the plain intention to do it well for someone.
Starting work. The first task of the day, handed over before the rest begin.
Hold onto this: offered work, the same tray or inbox with one thing added. That's today.

screen: `DAY 1626 COUNTS.` → `ORDINARY HOLINESS · 6 OF 80.` → `TOMORROW: PRAY AT SET TIMES OR ANYTIME? WHICH DOES THE CHURCH PICK?`

howItsDone: Many Catholics begin the workday with a short offering of their work to God, and monasteries following the Rule of Saint Benedict set hours for work and prayer side by side.

fork.reveal: Paul starts with eating and drinking, then says whatsoever else you do. the plain task is exactly what can be offered.

original.note: Greek: to the glory of God, the end of Paul's line in 1 Corinthians 10:31.

trapdoor: what you thought: holy work means church work.
what it means: offered work: any task, even the plainest first one, done for God.
what a scholar hears: 1 Corinthians 10:31 closes Paul's argument about meat sacrificed to idols; the Rule of Benedict 48 sets hours for labor and reading.
guess: beginning the day's work by offering it to God
the very first day at a brand-new job
a blessing a priest gives a new business
recall: the road to work, walked as prayer

chat.meaning: Paul names eating and drinking first, then whatsoever else you do. Offered work is the same task with one thing added: whom it's for.

Corinth.meaning: a Greek port city whose church Paul wrote to

Rule of Saint Benedict.meaning: a guide for monastery life written by Saint Benedict

Douay-Rheims.meaning: an older English Catholic translation of the Bible
